parts.partTitle: Protobuf vs JSON: The Wire Format

beats.headline: Why is JSON killing your microservice latency?
beats.subline: Text-based protocols are expensive. Let's look at the binary alternative.
beats.narration: JSON is great for debugging, but at thousands of calls per second, parsing strings and repeating property names adds massive CPU overhead. gRPC solves this with Protobuf.

beats.title: JSON vs Protobuf Wire Format
beats.narration: JSON sends keys like order underscore id every single time. Protobuf uses compact field tags. Tags 1 through 15 fit in a single byte, drastically shrinking your payload size.

beats.title: Safe Schema Evolution

steps.explanation: Changing a tag number breaks binary compatibility. Always lock them in.
Prevents accidental reuse of retired fields that could corrupt data.

beats.narration: Never change a field's wire type or reuse a deleted tag. If you remove a field, mark it as reserved. This ensures old clients don't accidentally interpret new data as garbage.

beats.title: Optimizing Wire Size
beats.subtitle: How Protobuf saves bytes

nodes.label: Varint Encoding
nodes.detail: Small integers use 1 byte instead of 4 or 8

nodes.label: ZigZag Mapping
nodes.detail: Encodes negative numbers as small unsigned integers

nodes.label: Field Tagging
nodes.detail: No field names on the wire, just index IDs

beats.narration: Use sint32 for negative values. Standard int32 uses 10 bytes for negatives, but ZigZag mapping compresses them into just 1 or 2 bytes, keeping your wire traffic lean.

beats.title: Part 1 Summary
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next: HTTP/2 Multiplexing and the L4 Load Balancing trap →
beats.narration: Protobuf is the foundation. Next, we look at why HTTP/2 multiplexing is a game changer, and why your Kubernetes load balancer might be pinning all your traffic to one pod.

beats.headline: Why does your gRPC traffic ignore half your cluster?
beats.subline: The L4 load balancing trap is the #1 cause of uneven service distribution.
beats.narration: You scaled your backend to 10 pods, but only one is handling traffic. Why? Because gRPC uses long-lived HTTP/2 connections, and standard L4 balancers don't see the streams inside.

beats.title: HTTP/2 Multiplexing
beats.subtitle: Multiple streams, one TCP socket
beats.narration: HTTP/2 splits every RPC into binary frames tagged with a Stream ID. This allows multiple concurrent requests over a single TCP connection, eliminating the need for massive connection pools.

beats.title: L4 vs L7 Load Balancing

top.label: L4 (ClusterIP)
points: Pins all streams to one pod

beats.narration: L4 balancers route at the TCP level. Since gRPC keeps the connection open, the load balancer never sees the individual requests. Use an L7 proxy or headless services to fix this.

beats.title: Client-Side Load Balancing

steps.explanation: Uses DNS to discover all pod IPs for a headless service.
Distributes RPCs across available endpoints client-side.

beats.narration: Use a headless service and the round robin policy. This forces the client to resolve all pod IPs and rotate requests, bypassing the L4 pinning problem entirely.

beats.title: Part 2 Summary
takeaways: Use L7 proxies for stream awareness

beats.narration: Stop pinning your traffic. In Part 3, we implement the four gRPC streaming modes in Java and handle backpressure with virtual threads.

beats.headline: Unary is easy. What about bidirectional streaming?
beats.subline: Managing state and backpressure in Java requires careful observer handling.
beats.narration: gRPC supports four communication patterns. From simple unary calls to full-duplex bidirectional streams, here is how you handle them in Java without leaking memory.

beats.title: The Four gRPC Modes
beats.subtitle: From Unary to Full Duplex
beats.narration: Unary is standard. Server streaming is perfect for market ticks. Client streaming is for batch uploads. Bidirectional is for real-time sessions where both sides talk concurrently.

beats.title: Bidirectional Stream Implementation

steps.explanation: The core interface for asynchronous push-based communication.
Not thread-safe! Serialize writes if calling from multiple threads.

beats.narration: The StreamObserver is not thread-safe. If you are pushing events from multiple background threads, you must synchronize your calls to onNext to prevent corrupted frames.

beats.title: Java 21 Virtual Threads

steps.explanation: Offload blocking I/O to lightweight threads, not platform threads.

beats.narration: On Java 21, use virtual threads for your gRPC executor. It allows you to handle thousands of concurrent streams without exhausting your platform thread pool.

beats.title: Part 3 Summary
takeaways: Use Virtual Threads for blocking I/O
Four modes cover all sync/async needs

beats.headline: How do you stop a slow service from crashing your whole cluster?
beats.subline: Deadline propagation is the secret to building resilient distributed systems.
beats.narration: One slow service can hold connections open until your entire cluster dies. You need automatic deadline propagation and robust error handling to fail fast.

beats.title: Deadline Propagation
beats.subtitle: Fail fast across the call chain
beats.narration: When you set a deadline, gRPC propagates the remaining time in the headers. If a downstream service exceeds this, it is cancelled immediately, saving resources.

beats.title: ServerInterceptor for Auth

steps.explanation: Reject unauthenticated requests before they hit your service logic.
Bind identity to the request context, not ThreadLocal.

beats.narration: Never use ThreadLocal for auth; gRPC execution hops across threads. Use Context instead. It safely carries your user identity through the entire call lifecycle.

beats.title: Handling Status Codes
beats.caption: Map failures to standard gRPC codes
beats.narration: gRPC status codes are your contract. Use UNAVAILABLE for retriable network blips, but never retry on INVALID_ARGUMENT. Keep error descriptions clean—no stack traces.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
takeaways: Use Context for auth, not ThreadLocal
Map errors to canonical status codes
